papers.title: A homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the C-terminal of Tdrd5 causing early spermiogenesis arrest and azoospermia in mice.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: TDRD5 is a germ cell-specific RNA granule component that plays a crucial role in chromatoid body organization, piRNA biogenesis, and spermiogenesis. We previously identified a homozygous C-terminal nonsense mutation in TDRD5 in an infertile patient. While in vitro studies suggested the production of a stable truncated protein, the physiological consequences of this specific C-terminal truncation in vivo remain unknown.

PURPOSE: This study aimed to elucidate the in vivo pathogenicity of the TDRD5 C-terminal nonsense mutation and its underlying mechanism using a mouse model.

METHODS: We generated a Tdrd5 knock-in mouse carrying a premature termination mutation (Q764X) at the corresponding C-terminal region of murine TDRD5 using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing. The reproductive phenotype was assessed through fertility testing, histological analysis (H&E, PAS), and evaluation of apoptosis (TUNEL). The expression of TDRD5 protein was assessed by immunoblot analysis, and retrotransposon activity was examined by co-staining for LINE1 and the DNA damage marker γH2AX.

RESULTS: Homozygous Tdrd5Q764X/Q764X male mice exhibited infertility, reduced testis size, and azoospermia. Histological examination revealed spermiogenic arrest at the round spermatid stage with defective acrosome biogenesis. Contrary to in vitro findings, immunoblot analysis demonstrated the complete absence of both full-length and truncated TDRD5 proteins in Tdrd5Q764X/Q764X testes. In addition, the mutant testes exhibited aberrant LINE1 upregulation, increased γH2AX signals in spermatocytes, and elevated germ cell apoptosis, thereby phenocopying the defects observed in Tdrd5-/- mice.

CONCLUSION: Our findings demonstrated that the C-terminal nonsense mutation causes a loss-of-function phenotype in vivo. This study highlighted the indispensable role of the TDRD5 C-terminus in maintaining protein stability and ensuring successful spermiogenesis in mice.

papers.title: Transrectal approach to oocyte retrieval in a patient with vaginal cancer.
papers.abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To describe the pre-procedural planning and demonstrate the intra-procedural technique of transrectal ultrasound-guided oocyte retrieval (TROR) in a patient with vaginal cancer.

DESIGN: Video article.

SETTING: University-affiliated fertility center.

SUBJECT(S): A 19-year-old virginal female with primary clear cell cancer of the vagina presented for fertility preservation. She was unable to tolerate a pelvic examination or transvaginal ultrasonography (TVUS) due to significant pain and bleeding. Her antral follicle count (AFC) and anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) was 37 and 67 pmol/L (9.38 ng/mL), respectively. Controlled ovarian stimulation (COS) was initiated with 150 units of recombinant follicle stimulating hormone (FSH) in a gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) antagonist protocol. Transabdominal ultrasonography (TAUS) on the 10th day of COS revealed 11 follicles measuring 17 mm or larger in both ovaries. TAUS also demonstrated access to only the lateral portion of the right ovary; access to the left ovary was limited significantly by the uterus and intervening vasculature. Given the short notice, a laparoscopic oocyte retrieval was not possible, and both transabdominal and transrectal retrieval of oocytes was proactively discussed. Bowel preparation was implemented the day before the retrieval. The patient gave consent for publication and posting of the video online including social media, the journal website, scientific literature websites (such as PubMed, ScienceDirect, Scopus, etc.) and other applicable sites.

INTERVENTION: TROR 36 hours after ovulatory trigger.

MAIN OUTCOME MEASURES: Total and mature oocyte yield after TROR.

RESULTS: A 7 mHz vaginal transducer with diameter of 23.8 mm, covered with a sterile cover, and copious lubrication was gently introduced into the rectum. Both ovaries were visualized easily. A 17 G, 25-cm single lumen needle was used for follicular aspiration. Twenty nine oocytes were retrieved, of which 28 mature oocytes were cryopreserved. The patient was prescribed oral levofloxacin and metronidazole for 5 days post-TROR. She had an uneventful postoperative course and began her oncologic treatment shortly after.

CONCLUSION: TROR is a viable alternative to the transabdominal and/or laparoscopic approach in patients with vaginal or cervical cancer. Despite its novelty, TROR should be performed only when transvaginal, transabdominal or laparoscopic oocyte retrieval is not safe or feasible.

papers.title: Effects of Polyendocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) on the Endometrium.
papers.abstract: Polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS), previously known as polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), is the most common reproductive, endocrine, and metabolic disorder affecting 11-13% of adolescent girls and women of reproductive age. Although anovulation has traditionally been considered the primary cause of PMOS-associated infertility, accumulating evidence demonstrates that impaired endometrial receptivity and decidualization also contribute substantially to embryo implantation failure, recurrent pregnancy loss, and other adverse pregnancy outcomes, including miscarriage, gestational diabetes, pregnancy-induced hypertension, preeclampsia, and preterm birth. In addition to reproductive disorders, women with PMOS also commonly present with obesity, insulin resistance, and other long-term health conditions. This review summarizes current knowledge of the cellular and molecular mechanisms by which PMOS disrupts endometrial function. We discuss how hyperandrogenism, insulin resistance, obesity, and chronic inflammation, both independently and collectively, impair endometrial receptivity by altering androgen receptor (AR) signaling, glucose metabolism, extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling, immune homeostasis, cell-cell junctions, adhesion molecules, and key regulators of decidualization. We also highlight recent advances in transcriptomic and single-cell sequencing studies that have revealed cell type-specific alterations and molecular heterogeneity within the PMOS endometrium. Despite substantial progress, the mechanisms linking endocrine and metabolic abnormalities to impaired endometrial function remain incompletely understood. A better understanding of PMOS-associated endometrial dysfunction will facilitate the identification of novel therapeutic targets and improve embryo implantation success, pregnancy outcomes, and reproductive health in women with PMOS.

papers.title: Phospholipase C Zeta 1 Supports Post-Fertilization Embryo Development beyond Oocyte Activation: Evidence from Sperm mRNA Analysis and Functional Studies.
papers.abstract: Phospholipase C zeta 1 (PLCZ1), the principal sperm-derived factor, initiates intracellular calcium (Ca²⁺) oscillations at fertilization; however, its contribution to post-fertilization embryonic development remains unclear. This study investigated whether PLCZ1 protein and PLCZ1 mRNA levels influence embryo quality beyond their canonical role in oocyte activation (OA) in human assisted reproductive technology (ART) cycles and functionally examined this hypothesis using a mouse embryo model. Sperm PLCZ1 protein expression assessed in 48 infertile couples undergoing in vitro fertilization/intracytoplasmic sperm injection significantly correlated with clinical fertilization rates. Sperm PLCZ1 mRNA levels were significantly higher in samples from patients producing good quality embryos (Grade A or B) than in those from patients yielding poor quality embryos (Grade C and D, p < 0.001), independent of paternal age. Functionally, microinjection of human PLCZ1 (hPLCZ1) cRNA into mouse metaphase II oocytes induced repetitive Ca²⁺ oscillations, thus confirming biological activity. Injecting hPLCZ1 cRNA into mouse pronuclear-stage embryos following parthenogenetic activation significantly enhanced blastocyst development compared with that in diethyl pyrocarbonate-treated water-injected controls (p = 0.0101), achieving rates comparable to those of diploid embryos generated using cytochalasin B treatment. These findings are consistent with a dual-component model in which sperm-derived PLCZ1 protein initiates OA at fertilization, while sperm-derived PLCZ1 mRNA is translationally competent within the oocyte and may contribute to sustained post-fertilization PLCZ1 activity and preimplantation developmental competence. Because the functional data were generated with exogenous cRNA rather than by manipulating the endogenous sperm transcript, this model remains a hypothesis that will require loss-of-function validation in future work. Despite limitations such as the moderate clinical sample size and use of mRNA as a surrogate for PLCZ1 protein in clinical samples, sperm PLCZ1 mRNA quantification represents a candidate, hypothesis-generating biomarker for embryo quality that warrants prospective validation.

papers.title: Does blastocyst transfer have a higher live birth rate than cleavage-stage embryo transfer in patients with delayed in vitro blastocyst development?
papers.abstract:
RESEARCH QUESTION: When embryo cohorts exhibit delayed blastocyst development, with only slow-developing day 6 (D6) blastocysts available for transfer, does blastocyst transfer achieve a higher live birth rate (LBR) than cleavage-stage embryo transfer?

METHODS: A modified blastocyst culture strategy was applied in freeze-all cycles. Specifically, one or two good-quality embryos were cryopreserved on day 3 (D3) as a backup, while an equal or greater number of good-quality embryos were cultured to the blastocyst stage. Among freeze-all patients managed with this strategy, 275 patients were identified who had only D6 blastocysts available for transfer, with no transferable day 5 (D5) blastocysts following extended in vitro culture. Cumulative LBR after one oocyte retrieval over 2 years and pregnancy outcomes in the first frozen-thawed embryo transfer (FET) cycles were compared between groups with priority transfer of backup D3 cleavage-stage embryos versus top-graded D6 blastocysts.

RESULTS: The cumulative LBR was not significantly different between the group with priority transfer of backup cryopreserved D3 embryos and the group with priority transfer of top-quality D6 blastocysts [50.6% vs. 48.4%; adjusted odds ratio (aOR), 0.759; 95% CI, 0.384-1.499; p = 0.427]. In the first FET cycles, transfer of top-graded D6 blastocysts did not yield a higher LBR compared with transfer of backup cryopreserved D3 embryos [36.3% vs. 43.5%; aOR, 0.601; 95% CI, 0.299-1.208; p = 0.153]. Subgroup analyses showed no significant differences in LBR between the two groups following either single embryo/blastocyst transfer (SET/SBT) (37.0% vs. 36.4%; aOR, 0.922; 95% CI, 0.234-3.634; p = 0.907) or double embryo/blastocyst transfer (DET/DBT) (35.4% vs. 44.6%; aOR, 0.493; 95% CI, 0.213-1.138; p = 0.097). No statistically significant differences were observed in clinical pregnancy rate, obstetric complications, or neonatal outcomes between the two groups in the first FET cycles.

CONCLUSIONS: When embryo cohorts exhibit delayed development at the blastocyst stage, blastocyst transfer does not result in a higher LBR and therefore may not confer an advantage in achieving live birth sooner compared with the transfer of good-quality cleavage-stage embryos.

papers.title: Does time-lapse imaging (TLI) of embryos improve reproductive outcomes in in vitro fertilisation (IVF)/intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI)? Individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis.
papers.abstract:
BACKGROUND: Time‑lapse imaging (TLI) systems may improve the success of in vitro fertilisation (IVF)/intracytoplasmic sperm injection (ICSI) by enabling undisturbed embryo culture and/or providing morphokinetic data to refine embryo selection. Despite several trials and aggregate meta-analyses showing uncertainty of benefit, there is little translation of evidence into guidelines. Heterogeneity in participant populations and algorithms used for TLI, although acknowledged in aggregate meta-analyses, remains unaddressed.

OBJECTIVE AND RATIONALE: We conducted an individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis to assess whether TLI improves reproductive outcomes and if effects vary by women or intervention characteristics. Our IPD meta-analysis enhances statistical power, allowing precise estimation of treatment effects and identification of subgroup differences. It overcomes the limitations of aggregate meta-analyses by enabling harmonised adjustment by participant-level baseline risk, testing treatment-covariate interactions and provides a comprehensive evaluation of TLI by leveraging diverse datasets from multiple studies that assess both undisturbed culture and morphokinetic-based embryo selection. The study implements rigorous data integrity and consistency checks to enhance the reliability and trustworthiness of its findings.

SEARCH METHODS: We conducted an IPD meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) in women undergoing IVF/ICSI that used TLI systems. We evaluated overall TLI (undisturbed culture and morphokinetic-based embryo selection), undisturbed culture alone, and morphokinetic-based embryo selection alone. The primary outcome was live birth after a first fresh or frozen embryo transfer; other outcomes included clinical pregnancy, biochemical pregnancy loss, miscarriage, multiple pregnancy, minor and major congenital malformations, birth weight, and gestational age at birth. We included trials from the 2019 Cochrane review and updated searches of MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, and CENTRAL from 7 January 2019 to 9 May 2025 and repeated the search on 28 July 2026. We requested IPD from the authors of included trials. We assessed study-level risk of bias using the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool for RCTs (ROB2) and undertook integrity assessment of included studies. We performed a two-stage IPD meta-analysis. Results are presented as adjusted odds ratios (aOR) with 95% confidence intervals and adjusted absolute risk difference (aRD) estimates in a modified intention-to-treat population with pre-specified subgroup and sensitivity analyses.

OUTCOMES: We included IPD from eight trials (n = 5642) for the primary analysis and added aggregate data from eight trials (n = 3452) for a sensitivity analysis. ROB2 assessment raised no concerns with the IPD-included trials. High-certainty evidence indicated no clinically important difference in live birth rates for overall TLI versus standard embryo incubation and selection (four trials, n = 2913, aOR 0.97, 95% CI 0.81-1.15, absolute risk difference(ARD) -0.7%, 95% CI -4.9% to 3.4%), undisturbed versus disturbed embryo culture (five trials, n = 2971, aOR 1.02, 95% CI 0.84-1.23, ARD 0.5%, 95% CI -4.1% to 5.0%), or morphokinetic-based versus standard embryo selection (three trials, n = 2937, aOR 0.92, 95% CI 0.78-1.07, ARD -2.0%, 95% CI -5.7% to 1.6%). No interaction was observed between the intervention effect and age, duration of undisturbed culture, day of embryo transfer, or type of embryo transfer (fresh or frozen) for live birth. Rates of clinical pregnancy, miscarriage, biochemical pregnancy loss, birthweight, and gestational age were similar between TLI systems and standard care across all comparisons.

WIDER IMPLICATIONS: High-certainty evidence indicates that live birth rates with time-lapse imaging are comparable to those with standard embryo incubation and selection, providing a robust basis for clinical practice and guideline development.

REGISTRATION NUMBER: PROSPERO CRD42024564332.

papers.title: Automation of sperm preparation, oocyte retrieval and denudation, ICSI, and vitrification in IVF: insights from a proof-of-concept study.
papers.abstract:
STUDY QUESTION: Can key embryological procedures, including sperm preparation, oocyte retrieval and denudation, ICSI, and blastocyst vitrification, be automated?

SUMMARY ANSWER: Individual automated systems enabling sperm preparation, oocyte retrieval and denudation, ICSI, and embryo vitrification demonstrated feasibility in a small proof-of-concept study.

WHAT IS KNOWN ALREADY: Automated systems for specific IVF procedures have shown promise, with recent reports of successful births following automated gamete isolation and ICSI.

STUDY DESIGN, SIZE, DURATION: Prospective proof-of-concept study evaluating five automated systems nicknamed 'Pearls'. Each system automated one of the following procedures: sperm preparation via swim-up (Pearl 1-SU); sperm preparation by a dish-based approach called horizontal swim-out (Pearl 1-HSO), oocyte retrieval, and denudation (Pearl 2); sperm selection and laser immobilization and piezo-ICSI (Pearl 3); and blastocyst vitrification (Pearl 5). The study enrolled patients undergoing treatment at Hope IVF, Guadalajara, Mexico, between October 2023 and October 2024, with data collection on pregnancy outcomes being completed in October 2025.

PARTICIPANTS/MATERIALS, SETTING, METHODS: Thirty-two patients or oocyte donors each underwent a single egg retrieval following minimal or mild ovarian stimulation. One patient was excluded from the study due to poor ovarian response. Oocytes were prospectively allocated to treatment with a single automated system: Pearl 1-SU (n = 20), Pearl 1-HSO (n = 37), Pearl 2 (n = 34), Pearl 3 (n = 57), with sibling oocytes treated manually per standard protocol. In the case of the automated vitrification system (Pearl 5), sibling blastocysts produced following manual ICSI were assigned to either manual or automated (n = 10) vitrification.

MAIN RESULTS AND THE ROLE OF CHANCE: Pearl 1-SU and Pearl 1-HSO automated sperm preparation systems achieved fertilization rates of 90% (18/20) and 73% (27/37), and sibling oocytes injected with manually prepared sperm achieved 60% (6/10) and 75% (18/24) fertilization. Usable blastocyst rates were 55.5% (10/18) and 70.4% (19/27) for the automated systems, and 50% (3/6) and 66.7% (12/18) for manual preparation. Pearl 2 automated oocyte retrieval and denudation resulted in a fertilization rate of 79.4% (27/34) and a usable blastocyst rate of 48.1% (13/27); manual procedures achieved 66.7% (26/39) and 76.9% (20/26) fertilization and blastocyst formation rates, respectively. Pearl 3 automated ICSI resulted in a fertilization rate of 59.6% (34/57), while this rate in sibling oocytes injected manually was 80% (36/45). Usable blastocyst formation rates were 58.8% (20/34) for automated and 61.1% (22/36) for manual ICSI. Thirty-five single embryo transfers from the automation group resulted in 16 clinical pregnancies and 16 live births in 26 patients (Pearl 1-SU = 3/6; Pearl 1-HSO = 4/7; Pearl 2 = 4/7; Pearl 3 = 4/13; Pearl 5 = 1/2). Two extremely preterm deliveries in the Pearl 1 group, associated with severe pre-eclampsia and vaginal/urinary infection, respectively, led to neonatal and infant deaths. No transfers involved embryos from the manual group for Pearl 1. One embryo transfer from the manual group of Pearl 2 resulted in a negative pregnancy. In the Pearl 3 manual group, four single blastocyst transfers in four patients resulted in four live births; in the Pearl 5 manual control group, three transfers in three patients resulted in two negative pregnancy results and one early pregnancy loss.

LIMITATIONS, REASONS FOR CAUTION: The small sample size and pilot design of this study do not allow statistical comparisons between sibling oocytes from automated and manual treatment groups. The automated systems did not achieve complete autonomy, and several tasks required direct operator intervention or execution through digital control. Pearl 5 encountered technical limitations that require further development before additional clinical evaluation. Although the two extremely preterm births that led to neonatal and infant deaths occurred in the context of clear obstetric complications, they compel collection and analysis of extensive technical and biological data from the automated systems in future studies and close monitoring of all pregnancies and births resulting from these novel procedures.

WIDER IMPLICATIONS OF THE FINDINGS: These results show the feasibility of integrating individual automated systems into an IVF laboratory as experimental standalone tools, allowing a stepwise evaluation. The modular approach, once shown to be efficacious, may provide a practical pathway toward broader laboratory automation and enable laboratories to address specific bottlenecks and standardize operations.

FUNDING: The study was sponsored by Conceivable Life Sciences, New York, NY, USA.

DISCLOSURES: A.C.-B. is an employee, shareholder, and company officer at Conceivable Life Sciences and a shareholder in IVF 2.0 and Hope IVF Mexico. A.V.A. has no conflicts of interest to declare. Pending applications cover automated dish preparation technology (A.C.-B., G.M.-R., N.C.-B., M.A., A.M., J.C.), automated oocyte denudation (A.C.-B., G.M.-R., N.C.-B., J.C.), automated vitrification systems (A.C.-B., E.H.-M., N.C.-B., A.M., J.C.), and cumulus-oocyte complex detection technology (A.C.-B., G.M.-R., J.C.).

papers.title: Ovarian gonadotoxicity and gonadoprotection: a narrative review.
papers.abstract: Chemotherapy-induced gonadotoxicity is a serious concern for cancer survivors, particularly children and women of reproductive age. The mechanisms by which chemotherapy depletes the ovarian reserve and impairs fertility are multifactorial. Chemotherapy can induce apoptosis of growing and primordial follicles, as well as excessive activation of primordial follicles, leading to burnout of the ovarian reserve. Stromal damage may further exacerbate these effects. Preclinical studies have aimed to safeguard the ovary against chemotherapy by targeting follicular apoptosis through inhibition of specific pathway mediators (tyrosine kinase inhibitors, serine/threonine kinase inhibitors, sphingolipids) or use of mesenchymal-stem-cell-derived factors, specific microRNA and antioxidant molecules. Other studies have focused on inhibiting follicular activation by targeting direct pathways (e.g. phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase and mammalian target of rapamycin modulators) or indirect regulators (e.g. anti-Müllerian hormone). Finally, some approaches aim to protect the ovarian stroma, which may be crucial to preserving ovarian function. The objective of this article is to provide an updated overview of the effects of chemotherapy on the ovary, and summarize current and emerging gonadoprotective strategies. Although numerous preclinical studies have reported encouraging results, further research is needed before these approaches can be considered safe and suitable for clinical application.

papers.title: Beyond anti-Müllerian hormone or antral follicle count alone: anti-Müllerian hormone and antral follicle count ratio as marker of ovarian responsiveness to gonadotrophins.
papers.abstract:
RESEARCH QUESTION: Is the anti-Müllerian hormone to antral follicle count ratio (AMH‒AFC) associated with ovarian responsiveness to gonadotrophins during ovarian stimulation?

DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study including 2162 IVF and intracytoplasmic sperm injection ovarian stimulation cycles carried out using a gonadotrophin releasing hormone antagonist protocol at a tertiary IVF centre. Associations between the AMH‒AFC ratio and ovarian responsiveness were evaluated with multiple regression analysis using the follicular output rate (FOR), follicle-to-oocyte index (FOI) and oocytes retrieved.

RESULTS: The AMH‒AFC ratio showed significant positive correlation with both FOI (r = 0.62, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.65) and FOR (r = 0.62, 95% CI 0.59 to 0.65; both P < 0.001), with stronger associations than AMH or AFC when assessed individually. When stratified by AMH‒AFC quartiles, a progressive increase was observed in pre-ovulatory follicles, retrieved oocytes, metaphase II oocytes, FOI and FOR across higher ratio categories. In multivariable analyses adjusted for age, body mass index and gonadotrophin dose, the AMH‒AFC ratio explained a greater proportion of variance in FOI and FOR than either marker alone. The combined use of AMH and AFC, however, remained superior for predicting absolute oocyte and metaphase II yield.

CONCLUSIONS: The AMH‒AFC ratio is associated with dynamic markers of ovarian responsiveness during ovarian stimulation and may provide complementary information regarding follicular sensitivity to gonadotrophins. Although it does not replace the combined use of AMH and AFC for predicting absolute oocyte yield, the ratio may help identify women with discordant ovarian reserve profiles who are at risk of suboptimal ovarian response despite apparently reassuring follicle counts.

papers.title: From morphology to molecular validation: ethical re-evaluation of 3PN-derived embryos.
papers.abstract: In assisted reproduction, the presence of three pronuclei (3PN) in zygotes has long been considered a clear indicator of abnormal fertilization. Current international guidelines recommend the systematic discarding of 3PN-derived embryos due to presumed triploidy and the associated risk of molar pregnancy. However, some studies have demonstrated that a proportion of 3PN-derived embryos exhibit a diploid and euploid chromosomal constitution, with reports of healthy live births following the transfer of genetically confirmed diploid 3PN-derived embryos, and no documented cases of molar pregnancy. These findings challenge the theoretical risks inferred from naturally conceived triploid conceptuses and raise concerns regarding the validity of extrapolating risk estimates from spontaneous pregnancies to assisted reproduction settings. Morphology-based exclusion criteria may result in the discarding of potentially viable embryos despite molecular confirmation of chromosomal normality, thereby raising ethical issues related to beneficence and reproductive autonomy, particularly in patients with limited embryo availability. These considerations highlight the need for structured, ethically governed research pathways capable of generating the robust clinical evidence required to inform future guideline evaluation. In this paper, a cautious but proactive framework is proposed, incorporating blastocyst culture, validation by preimplantation genetic testing for aneuploidies, ethics committee oversight, extended informed consent and long-term follow-up to balance safety with innovation.

papers.title: Clinical implications of zygotes showing 2.1 pronuclei: an ASPIRE Embryology Special Interest Group committee opinion.
papers.abstract: Atypical fertilisation patterns such as 2.1 pronuclei (2.1PN), defined by two normally sized pronuclei and an additional smaller pronucleus, present a clinical challenge due to inconsistent classification and uncertainty regarding their development and genetic potential. This scoping review aims to synthesise the existing evidence, identify gaps in the literature and propose a committee opinion on 2.1PN zygotes, including a working provisional definition, to guide clinical practice and future studies. A PubMed search for studies reporting 2.1PN zygotes and their developmental and clinical outcomes was conducted in May 2025. This review shows conflicting evidence regarding blastulation rates between 2.1PN and 2PN zygotes, and findings on preimplantation genetic testing and live birth rates remain inconclusive due to limited study numbers and sample sizes. Regardless, 2.1PN zygotes should be distinguished from classic 3PN zygotes, cultured to the blastocyst stage and genetically assessed if available. Based on current evidence and expert consensus, we propose a provisional working definition of the 2.1PN zygote to support standardised classification. Current evidence suggests that 2.1PN zygotes can be viable and warrant differentiation from 3PN zygotes. Future research should clarify the mechanisms underlying 2.1PN formation, determine neonatal and longer-term health outcomes following 2.1PN-derived embryo transfer and validate findings in larger cohorts.

papers.title: Do blastocysts which form on day 4 have an altered pregnancy potential? A narrative review.
papers.abstract: The clinical pregnancy rate for assisted reproductive technology (ART) has remained static for several years. Although the reasons for this are multifactorial, reliable selection of the single optimal embryo for transfer remains a challenge. Embryo selection currently relies on visual assessment, with judgements based on cellular morphology and timing of developmental milestones. Accepted ART practice considers that embryos should reach blastocyst stage on day 5 post oocyte insemination, and this is assumed to be the optimal day on which to utilize the embryo. However, the advent of time-lapse imaging has revealed a variable frequency of blastocyst formation, ranging from day 4 to day 7. Despite current practice not involving routine assessment on day 4, emerging evidence suggests that embryos which reach blastocyst stage and are utilized on day 4 may have an improved chance of pregnancy. Reducing time in vitro could also have benefits for ongoing pregnancy and offspring health. This review provides a clinical perspective on the relationship between the day of blastocyst formation and pregnancy outcomes. Reflecting on this evidence will allow clinical professionals to consider both monitoring and utilizing blastocysts on day 4 in order to improve pregnancy success outcomes after ART.
